summary: Introduces a PCEP extension that associates a group of LSPs for the purpose of computing diverse (disjoint) paths. A client can tell a PCE that an LSP belongs to a given disjoint association group.

eli5.summary: If two buses must not share any road in case one is blocked, this tells the planner to keep them apart.

questions: how to compute disjoint lsps with pcep
what is a disjoint association group
what is the p flag in pcep disjointness
subtitle: How PCEP tells a path computation element that a group of LSPs must take different routes through the network.

tldr.problem: Operators often must give a customer two end-to-end paths that do not share links, nodes or fate, but PCEP had no standard way to say that a set of LSPs belong together and must be disjoint.
tldr.mechanism: A new Disjoint Association type for the ASSOCIATION object groups the LSPs, a DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV states what kind of disjointness is required, and a DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV reports what was achieved.
tldr.outcome: A PCE that sees LSPs in the same Disjoint Association Group can compute them to be disjoint, strictly or with relaxation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 8800 is a Proposed Standard, and it is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Disjoint Paths
sections.content:
Path diversity is described as a very common use case in IP/MPLS networks, especially for layer 2 transport over MPLS. A customer may ask the operator for two end-to-end disjoint paths across its core and use them as primary and backup, or active and active. The LSPs may start at the same or different head ends and end at the same or different tail ends.

The RFC lists four levels of disjointness:

  • Link: the LSPs use different links.
  • Node: the LSPs use different nodes.
  • SRLG: the LSPs use links that share no Shared Risk Link Group, so no common shared fate, but may use common nodes.
  • Node+SRLG: different nodes and no common shared fate.

When LSPs start at different head ends, distributed computation of diverse paths can be difficult. A centralized PCE ensures disjointness, correctness and simplicity.
sections.eli5: A school can send two buses to the same place, but if both use the same bridge and it closes, both are stuck. So the planner has to pick different bridges, different towns or different power lines.

sections.title: The Disjoint Association Group
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the generic LSP grouping mechanism of RFC 8697. It defines a new Association type called Disjoint Association (type 2, or DAT) for the ASSOCIATION object. A group is identified by the Association Type, Association ID, Association Source and, if present, the Global Association Source or Extended Association ID. The Association ID field is limited to 65535, and the local choice of Association Source, such as the PCE address, helps to overcome that limit.

Both sides MUST advertise DAT in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV in the OPEN object before the group is used in PCEP messages. The type is both dynamic and operator-configured, and the Operator-configured Association Range MUST be set for it.

A group can have two or more LSPs, but a PCE may handle only a limited number. If it receives more, it SHOULD apply disjointness to only a subset, chosen by local policy. One LSP MAY belong to several groups; if the PCE cannot compute for that, it MUST NOT add the LSP and MUST return a PCErr with Error-Type 26 and Error-value 7 (Cannot join the association group).
sections.eli5: A group is a team name written on each LSP. Everyone with the same team name must stay apart from each other, and both sides must agree they understand team names before using them.

sections.title: The Disjointness TLVs
sections.content:
A Disjoint Association Group MUST carry a DISJOINTNESS-CONFIGURATION TLV (type 46, fixed length 4 bytes). It can also carry a DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV, a VENDOR-INFORMATION TLV and an OF-List TLV. If a peer receives a group without the configuration TLV, it SHOULD reply with a PCErr of Error-Type 6 and Error-value 15.

The flags in the configuration TLV are:

  • L (Link Diverse): the paths MUST NOT have any link in common.
  • N (Node Diverse): the paths MUST NOT have any node in common.
  • S (SRLG Diverse): the paths MUST NOT share any SRLG.
  • P (Shortest Path): the path of this LSP SHOULD first satisfy all constraints and objective functions without the diversity constraint.
  • T (Strict Disjointness): if disjoint paths cannot be found, the PCE MUST return no path for the LSPs that could not be disjoint. When unset, the PCE may relax disjointness.

Unassigned bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. All LSPs in a group MUST use the same combination of T, S, N and L flags, otherwise the peer MUST NOT add the LSP and MUST reply with Error-Type 26 and Error-value 6 (Association information mismatch).

The DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV (type 47) has the same format and is sent from PCE to PCC. It reports what was achieved: L, N and S are set if requested and met, and P marks a shortest path. The T flag has no meaning there and MUST NOT be set.
sections.eli5: Each LSP carries a little form with tick boxes: do not share roads, do not share towns, do not share power lines, be the best route, and be strict. The planner fills in a second form saying what it managed to do.

sections.title: Objective Functions and the P Flag
sections.content:
An objective function (OF) can steer how the PCE computes. It goes in the OF-List TLV of RFC 5541. A sender SHOULD put a single OF-code in it, and the receiver MUST consider only the first. Three new OF-codes minimize sharing: MSL (code 15, shared links), MSS (code 16, shared SRLGs) and MSN (code 17, shared nodes). If the OF-List is present, the first code MUST be one of these, or the speaker MUST respond with PCErr Error-Type 10 and Error-value 32 (Incompatible OF code).

The P flag handles primary and backup cases. LSPs with P set are computed first as if there were no disjointness constraint. Then the LSPs with P unset are computed around them. The relationship becomes one-sided. In the RFC example, a primary LSP PE1 to PE2 takes the best path and the other LSP is placed on a costlier but link-disjoint path through PE3, R5, R6 and PE4. The RFC warns that P, like any extra constraint, lowers the chance of finding disjoint paths. If router R5 is down and P is set, there is no room for the second LSP, and with equal-cost choices the implementation should aim for a path that allows disjointness.
sections.eli5: If one bus must take the fastest road, it picks first. The second bus then goes around it, even if its trip is longer. The planner can also be told to share as little as possible when keeping apart is not fully possible.

sections.title: Working with SVEC
sections.content:
PCEP already has the SVEC object (RFC 5440) to link a set of synchronized path requests. A PCReq MAY use both SVEC and ASSOCIATION objects. The PCE MUST consider both, including their flags, and try to find a path that meets both. If no such path is possible it MUST send a PCRep with a NO-PATH object.

The two behave differently over time. An SVEC is considered only once on receipt of the PCReq, while a group in the stateful database keeps influencing later changes. The RFC's examples show that a change to an LSP in the group affects the other LSP, but a change to one only in the SVEC does not. SVEC diversity flags can also combine with an OF: node-diverse SVEC with OF=MSS gives full node diversity with as much SRLG diversity as possible.
sections.eli5: There is an older way to say two trips must be separate, but it only counts at the moment of asking. Groups keep watching, so later changes still matter. Both can be used together.

sections.title: When Disjointness Fails
sections.content:
With T set, if disjointness cannot be ensured the PCE MUST answer a PCReq with a PCRep holding a NO-PATH object. For a PCRpt it MUST return a PCErr with Error-Type 26 and Error-value 7. If a network event makes strict disjointness impossible, the PCE MUST send a PCUpd with an empty ERO, and MAY add a NO-PATH-VECTOR TLV.

Two new NO-PATH-VECTOR flag bits are added: bit 11 means no disjoint path was found for this LSP, and bit 10 means the requested disjoint computation is not supported.

With T unset, the PCE may relax. If an objective function was requested it uses it. Otherwise it may reduce the level of disjointness as it sees fit, and the achieved level is reported through the DISJOINTNESS-STATUS TLV. A mechanism to fully relax the constraint is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the rule is strict and no separate roads exist, the planner says no route. If the rule is relaxed, it does its best and tells you how separate the routes ended up.

sections.title: Security and Operations
sections.content:
The new Association type adds no new security concerns beyond those of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 7470 and RFC 8697. Still, a spurious LSP added to a group could trigger recomputation and setup of every LSP in it, which could overwhelm the PCE and the network. A spurious LSP can also carry inconsistent flags and make allocation fail for the legitimate LSPs. Because associations show relationships between LSPs, an eavesdropper could learn about the network topology. Securing the PCEP session with TLS (RFC 8253) is RECOMMENDED.

Operationally, an implementation SHOULD let the operator configure groups and parameters, view the groups, and set local policies. It SHOULD also provide counters, such as the number of groups and failures, log failures like incompatible flags, and allow a limit on the number of LSPs per group.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker who sneaks a fake bus into the team could make the planner redo everything. Anyone watching the team lists could also learn how the roads connect. A locked connection helps.

items.label: Link Diverse
items.desc: Paths MUST NOT have any link in common.

items.label: Node Diverse
items.desc: Paths MUST NOT have any node in common.

items.label: SRLG Diverse
items.desc: Paths MUST NOT share any SRLG.

items.label: Shortest Path
items.desc: Compute this LSP first, ignoring the diversity constraint.

items.label: Strict Disjointness
items.desc: If disjoint paths cannot be found, return no path.
